items.value: Statement-I is correct (India withdraws over a quarter of the world's groundwater) but Statement-II is incorrect — that extraction is for irrigation, not drinking water and sanitation
items.reasoning: Statement-I is correct: India is by a wide margin the world's largest groundwater user, and the UN World Water Development Report 2022 on groundwater records its annual withdrawal as more than a quarter of the global total. Statement-II is false on the use to which that water is put — the overwhelming majority of India's groundwater abstraction, of the order of nine-tenths, goes to irrigation, while domestic drinking water and sanitation account for a small fraction. So the second statement supplies a purported justification that the actual pattern of use contradicts.

items.value: Only two are correct — the Union's duty to protect States against internal disturbance (1) and the preventive-detention exclusion from the right to counsel (2); POTA made police confessions admissible
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: Article 355 makes it the duty of the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance. Statement 2 is correct: Article 22(3)(b) provides that clauses (1) and (2) of Article 22 — which include the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner — do not apply to a person detained under a preventive detention law. Statement 3 is wrong and reverses the position: Section 32 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2002 expressly made a confession recorded by a police officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police admissible in evidence, notwithstanding the Indian Evidence Act — one of the Act's most criticised features. Runner-up is A if statement 2's phrasing about the State 'providing' counsel were read as inaccurate.

items.value: Somalia — decades of civil strife plus drought, in the news for severe famine conditions
items.reasoning: Somalia has endured state collapse, insurgency and civil conflict for over three decades, and successive failed rainy seasons combined with that conflict pushed parts of the country to the brink of declared famine, with severe food insecurity dominating humanitarian reporting. Angola's civil war ended in 2002 and it has not been in the news for famine; Costa Rica and Ecuador are stable Latin American states with no comparable civil strife or famine.

items.value: Both are correct — BMCs are central to India's access-and-benefit-sharing framework and may levy collection fees
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the Nagoya Protocol's object is fair and equitable sharing of benefits from the use of genetic resources, and in India that is operationalised through the National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Boards and, at the local level, Biodiversity Management Committees, which maintain the People's Biodiversity Registers documenting local resources and associated traditional knowledge. Statement 2 is correct: under the Biological Diversity Act a BMC must be consulted on decisions about the use of biological resources within its jurisdiction, and it may levy charges by way of collection fees from any person accessing or collecting a biological resource for commercial purposes from that area. Runner-up is A, if the BMC's role in benefit-sharing decisions were treated as purely advisory rather than determinative.

items.value: Only statement 4 is correct — Puducherry's per-MLA vote value exceeds Arunachal Pradesh's because its population-to-seats ratio is higher
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: Article 54 confines the electoral college to the ELECTED members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies, so nominated members are excluded. Statement 2 is wrong because the seat count sits in the DENOMINATOR — the value of an MLA's vote is the State's 1971 population divided by the number of elected seats, divided by a thousand — so for a given population more seats means a lower value per MLA. Statement 3 is wrong: Kerala's per-MLA value works out to about 152 against Madhya Pradesh's 131, so Kerala's is the greater. Statement 4 is correct in both its claim and its reason: Puducherry has roughly the same 1971 population as Arunachal Pradesh spread over half as many seats, giving values of about 16 against 8 — which incidentally also disproves statement 2.

items.value: Archaeological excavations
items.reasoning: All five were antiquarians and archaeologists connected with survey and excavation work in colonial India, largely in the south. James Burgess headed the Archaeological Survey of India; Alexander Rea and A. H. Longhurst served as its superintendents in the Madras circle and excavated Buddhist and temple sites; Walter Elliot was an administrator-antiquarian associated with the Amaravati sculptures; and Robert Sewell, best known for his study of Vijayanagara, compiled antiquarian and archaeological lists for the Madras Presidency. None is connected with the press, church building or railway construction.

items.value: Only two are correctly matched — Bhaja (Buddhist) and Sittanavasal (Jain); Besnagar is not a Shaivite cave shrine
items.reasoning: Pair 1 is wrong on both counts: Besnagar near Vidisha is famous for the Heliodorus pillar, a Garuda standard raised in honour of Vasudeva and therefore a VAISHNAVITE monument, and it is a free-standing pillar site, not a cave shrine. Pair 2 is correct: the Bhaja caves in Maharashtra are an early Buddhist rock-cut group with a chaitya hall and viharas. Pair 3 is correct: Sittanavasal in Tamil Nadu is a Jain rock-cut cave temple, celebrated for its murals.

items.value: Both correct, and the 1905 Swadeshi Movement launch is precisely why 7th August was chosen for National Handloom Day
items.reasoning: Statement-I is correct: 7th August is observed as National Handloom Day, first celebrated in 2015. Statement-II is correct: the Swadeshi Movement was formally launched at a meeting in the Calcutta Town Hall on 7 August 1905, in response to the proposed partition of Bengal. The date was selected for the handloom observance precisely to commemorate that movement, which promoted indigenous production and handloom weaving — so Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I.

items.value: Statement-I is incorrect (600 mm x 400 mm is not one of the Flag Code's listed sizes) but Statement-II is correct (the ratio is 3:2)
items.reasoning: Statement-II is correct: the Flag Code of India, 2002 stipulates that the ratio of the length to the height of the National Flag shall be 3:2. Statement-I is a trap that satisfies the ratio while failing the schedule: the Code lists a fixed set of standard sizes running 6300x4200, 3600x2400, 2700x1800, 1800x1200, 1350x900, 900x600, 450x300, 225x150 and 150x100 millimetres, and 600x400 — though correctly proportioned at 3:2 — is not among them. Runner-up is B, which would follow if 600x400 were in fact a listed size, in which case Statement-II would state the ratio rule rather than explain the size.

items.value: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect — the Drafting Committee was constituted in August 1947, and 26 November 1949 is the date of adoption
items.reasoning: Statement-I is correct: Constitution Day is observed on 26th November each year, a practice formally begun in 2015, to promote awareness of constitutional values. Statement-II misstates what happened on that date. The Drafting Committee under Dr B. R. Ambedkar was set up by the Constituent Assembly on 29 August 1947. What occurred on 26 November 1949 was the ADOPTION of the Constitution by the Constituent Assembly — which is the actual reason the date was chosen.

items.value: Statement-I is correct (Switzerland is a leading gold exporter by value) but Statement-II is incorrect (it does not hold the second largest gold reserves)
items.reasoning: Statement-I is correct: Switzerland is the world's dominant gold refining centre, importing bullion and re-exporting refined gold, which places it among the top exporters of gold by value. Statement-II is false: by official gold reserves Switzerland ranks well outside the top two — the United States holds by far the largest holding, followed by Germany, with Italy, France, Russia and China also ahead of Switzerland. Its export standing rests on refining throughput, not on the size of its reserves.

items.value: Statement-I is correct (the US-EU Trade and Technology Council was launched) but Statement-II is incorrect — no such claim of bringing technology under their control was made
items.reasoning: Statement-I is correct: the United States and the European Union established the Trade and Technology Council in 2021 as a forum to coordinate on trade, technology standards, export controls, supply-chain resilience and emerging technologies. Statement-II is false: the declared purpose is cooperation on shared standards, values and secure supply chains, and neither party claims to be bringing technological progress or productivity 'under their control' — that framing is not part of the initiative's stated objectives.

items.value: Statement-I is incorrect (India's share of global merchandise exports is far below 3.2%) but Statement-II is correct
items.reasoning: Statement-II is correct: the Production-Linked Incentive scheme has drawn participation from a large number of domestic manufacturers and from foreign firms manufacturing in India, notably in electronics and mobile handsets. Statement-I is not: India's share of world exports of GOODS is of the order of 1.8 per cent, roughly half the figure quoted, though its share of world SERVICES exports is around 4 per cent — the statement appears to conflate the two. Runner-up is B, which would follow if the 3.2 per cent figure were accepted, since PLI is in any case not an explanation of an export share.

items.value: Only statement 1 is correct — the Stability and Growth Pact limits budget deficits; it has nothing to do with sharing infrastructure or technology
items.reasoning: The Stability and Growth Pact is a fiscal rulebook: it commits member states to keep the general government deficit within 3 per cent of GDP and public debt within 60 per cent of GDP, with a surveillance and corrective arm to enforce them. So statement 1 is correct. Statements 2 and 3 describe things the Pact does not do — pooling of infrastructure and sharing of technology are matters for other Union policies and programmes entirely, and no such obligation arises from this treaty framework.

items.value: None of the statements is correct — the GCM was not adopted by all UN members, is non-binding, and does not cover internal migration
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: adoption was not universal — a number of states voted against the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration and others abstained, with the United States having withdrawn from the process altogether. Statement 2 is wrong: the Compact is expressly a non-legally-binding cooperative framework, and it says so in its own text; its objectives are commitments of intent, not obligations. Statement 3 is wrong: the Compact concerns INTERNATIONAL migration and does not extend its objectives to internal migration or internally displaced persons, who are covered by a separate body of guidance.

items.value: Only two are correct — the auxiliary-to-police role (2) and the Border Wing Home Guards Battalions (3); Home Guards are raised under State, not Central, Acts
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is wrong: Home Guards are a State subject and are raised under the Home Guards Acts and Rules of the respective States and Union Territories, not under a Central Government Act, though the Centre supports the organisation. Statement 2 is correct and is the force's defining role — a voluntary auxiliary to the police in the maintenance of internal security, called out to assist in emergencies. Statement 3 is correct: Border Wing Home Guards Battalions have been raised in border States to serve as an auxiliary to the Border Security Force and help check infiltration along the international border and coastal stretches.

items.value: Only two pairs are correctly matched — uniform misuse under the Official Secrets Act and celebratory gunfire under the Arms (Amendment) Act; the second belongs to the Official Secrets Act, not the Evidence Act
items.reasoning: Pair 1 is correct: Section 6 of the Official Secrets Act, 1923 penalises using or wearing, without lawful authority, a naval, military, air force, police or other official uniform. Pair 2 is wrong: obstructing, knowingly misleading or otherwise interfering with a police officer or a member of the armed forces on duty is also dealt with by the Official Secrets Act, 1923, whereas the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 is a procedural statute governing what may be proved in court and creates no such offence. Pair 3 is correct: the Arms (Amendment) Act, 2019 inserted a specific penal provision for using a firearm in a rash or negligent manner or in celebratory gunfire so as to endanger human life or the personal safety of others.

items.value: None of the pairs is correctly matched — the three reasons have been rotated away from their regions
items.reasoning: North Kivu and Ituri are provinces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in the news for armed-group violence and the M23 insurgency, not for Armenia and Azerbaijan. Nagorno-Karabakh is the disputed enclave at the centre of the Armenia-Azerbaijan conflict — the reason printed against pair 1 — not the Mozambique insurgency, which concerns Cabo Delgado. Kherson and Zaporizhzhia are Ukrainian oblasts contested in the Russia-Ukraine war, not sites of an Israel-Lebanon dispute. No region is matched with its own reason.

items.value: Statement-I is correct (Israel has diplomatic relations with several Arab states) but Statement-II is incorrect — Israel never signed the Arab Peace Initiative
items.reasoning: Statement-I is correct: Israel has established diplomatic relations with Egypt and Jordan through their respective peace treaties and, more recently, with the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Morocco. Statement-II is false: the Arab Peace Initiative was a Saudi proposal adopted by the Arab League at its 2002 Beirut summit as an offer to Israel — full normalisation in exchange for withdrawal to the 1967 lines and a resolution of the refugee question. It was a unilateral League declaration, not a signed bilateral instrument, and Israel did not sign or accept it.

items.value: Only two pairs are correctly matched — Khel Ratna (four-year outstanding performance) and Dronacharya (coaches); Arjuna and Rashtriya Khel Protsahan Puraskar are misdescribed
items.reasoning: Pair 1 is correct: the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award recognises the most spectacular and outstanding performance by a sportsperson over the preceding four years. Pair 2 is wrong: the Arjuna Award is for consistently outstanding performance over a four-year period, whereas lifetime achievement is recognised by the Dhyan Chand Award. Pair 3 is correct: the Dronacharya Award honours eminent coaches who have successfully trained sportspersons or teams. Pair 4 is wrong: the Rashtriya Khel Protsahan Puraskar goes to corporate entities, public-sector undertakings and other organisations and individuals that have played a visible role in promoting and developing sport — the description printed against it again belongs to the Dhyan Chand Award.

items.value: Only two are correct — first Chess Olympiad in India (1) and the mascot 'Thambi' (2); the two trophies are named the wrong way round
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the 44th Chess Olympiad, held at Mahabalipuram near Chennai in 2022, was the first Chess Olympiad hosted by India. Statement 2 is correct: the official mascot was a knight named 'Thambi'. Statements 3 and 4 are both wrong because the trophy names have been interchanged — the Hamilton-Russell Cup goes to the winning team in the open section and the Vera Menchik Cup to the winners of the women's section, which is the reverse of what is printed.

items.value: None of the pairs is correctly matched — Donbas is in Ukraine, Kachin in Myanmar and Tigray in Ethiopia
items.reasoning: Donbas is the eastern industrial region of Ukraine at the centre of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, not Syria. Kachin is a state of northern Myanmar, long the site of an ethnic armed conflict, not Ethiopia. Tigray is the northern Ethiopian region devastated by civil war — the country printed against pair 2 — and certainly not North Yemen. Each region has been paired with the wrong country, so no pair is correct.

items.value: Successful coups
items.reasoning: Chad, Guinea, Mali and Sudan all saw the military seize power in a short span of years, part of the run of successful coups across the Sahel and West Africa that prompted suspensions from the African Union and regional bodies. The other options do not hold across all four: none of them was in the news collectively for rare-earth discoveries or Chinese military bases, and while Sahelian desertification affects Chad, Mali and Sudan, it does not connect Guinea, which lies on the Atlantic coast in the humid tropics.

items.value: All three — fertilizer plants, oil refineries and steel plants are all expected to be decarbonized using green hydrogen
items.reasoning: All three already consume large volumes of hydrogen made from fossil feedstock, so substituting green hydrogen directly abates their emissions. Fertilizer plants need hydrogen for ammonia synthesis; refineries need it for hydrocracking and desulphurisation; and steel plants can use hydrogen in place of coke as the reducing agent in direct-reduced-iron routes. These are precisely the hard-to-abate industries named as priority end-uses in hydrogen missions and roadmaps.

items.value: Both are correct — the G-20 began as a finance ministers' and central bank governors' forum, and digital public infrastructure is an Indian G-20 priority
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: the G-20 was created in 1999, in the wake of the Asian financial crisis, as a forum of finance ministers and central bank governors to discuss international economic and financial stability; the leaders' summit format came only later, from 2008. Statement 2 is correct: digital public infrastructure was among the priorities India set out for its G-20 presidency, showcasing population-scale digital identity, payments and data-exchange systems as a development model for other members.
